Evidence for Preserved Representations in Change Blindness (https://www.chabris.com/Simons2002.pdf)
citeturn9view1 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: application/pdf; Number of pages: 20; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://www.chabris.com/Simons2002.pdf","lineno":null}); Total lines: 743
L0@P0: Consciousness and Cognition 11, 78–97 (2002)
L1@P0: doi:10.1006/ccog.2001.0533, available online at http://www.idealibrary.com on
L2@P0: Evidence for Preserved Representations in Change Blindness
L3@P0: Daniel J. Simons,1 Christopher F. Chabris, and Tatiana Schnur
L4@P0: Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138
L5@P0: and
L6@P0: Daniel T. Levin
L7@P0: Kent State University
L8@P0: People often fail to detect large changes to scenes, provided that the changes occur
L9@P0: during a visual disruption. This phenomenon, known as ‘‘change blindness,’’ occurs both
L10@P0: in the laboratory and in real-world situations in which changes occur unexpectedly. The
L11@P0: pervasiveness of the inability to detect changes is consistent with the theoretical notion
L12@P0: that we internally represent relatively little information from our visual world from one
L13@P0: glance at a scene to the next. However, evidence for change blindness does not necessarily
L14@P0: imply the absence of such a representation—people could also miss changes if they fail
L15@P0: to compare an existing representation of the pre-change scene to the post-change scene.
L16@P0: In three experiments, we show that people often do have a representation of some aspects
L17@P0: of the pre-change scene even when they fail to report the change. And, in fact, they appear
L18@P0: to ‘‘discover’’ this memory and can explicitly report details of a changed object in response
L19@P0: to probing questions. The results of these real-world change detection studies are discussed
L20@P0: in the context of broader claims about change blindness.  2002 Elsevier Science (USA)
L21@P0: Our experience of a rich, stable visual world often leads to the intuitive belief
L22@P0: that our representations of that world are correspondingly detailed and precise. But
L23@P0: increasing evidence for ‘‘change blindness,’’ the inability to detect large changes to
L24@P0: scenes from one glance to the next, has inspired claims that little to no information
L25@P0: about the world is preserved in visual short term memory (e.g., O’Regan, 1992;
L26@P0: Rensink, 2000a, 2000b). Such claims have some historical precedents (e.g., Gibson,
L27@P0: 1986/1979; Hochberg, 1986; Stroud, 1955), but they do not necessarily follow from
L28@P0: change blindness. Change blindness could occur for many reasons, even when observers have representations of the pre-change scene (Simons, 2000b). For example,
L29@P0: change blindness could reflect a failure to compare representations of the pre- and
L30@P0: post-change scene. Here, we present evidence that supports this possibility by showing that some subjects who fail to report a change can subsequently report features
L31@P0: of the pre-change object when asked.
L32@P0: Almost all evidence for change blindness derives from situations in which a change
L33@P0: is produced during a visual disruption or distraction (see Simons, 2000b; Simons &
L34@P0: Levin, 1997 for reviews) which serves to mask the transient that could otherwise
L35@P0: attract attention to the change. In essence, such change detection tasks are akin to

L42@P1: asking observers to report their experience of a visual illusion: they assess how the
L43@P1: visual system breaks down, and in so doing, reveal the basic assumptions of the
L44@P1: visual system. By ‘‘breaking’’ a system, we can often gain a better understanding
L45@P1: of how that system normally functions. Although changes typically are accompanied
L46@P1: by a change signal, by producing changes without such a signal (however unnatural
L47@P1: the disruption), we can better determine how much information is represented across
L48@P1: views. When a change produces a signal, we do not need to compare the before and
L49@P1: after representations to detect the change—we only need to detect the signal. In
L50@P1: contrast, when the change produces no such signal, successful change detection requires a representation of the feature of the original display that changed as well as
L51@P1: a comparison of that representation to the changed display. That is, successful change
L52@P1: detection requires that something be preserved from the first display.
L53@P1: In a study using motion picture cuts as a visual disruption, nearly two thirds of
L54@P1: unsuspecting observers miss a change to the identity of the central actor (Levin &
L55@P1: Simons, 1997). In fact, observers often do not notice when a stranger they are talking
L56@P1: to is surreptitiously replaced by a different person (Levin, Simons, Angelone, &
L57@P1: Chabris, in press; Simons & Levin, 1998). In one such study, an experimenter approached a pedestrian to ask for directions. As the pedestrian provided directions,
L58@P1: two people carrying a door passed between the experimenter and the pedestrian,
L59@P1: temporarily blocking the pedestrian’s view. During this disruption, the first experimenter was replaced by a different person (Simons & Levin, 1998). Under these
L60@P1: conditions, half of the observers did not realize that they were talking to a new person
L61@P1: after the door passed by. Similar levels of change blindness occur when the pedestrian
L62@P1: is asked to take a photograph of the experimenter and the person-switch occurs while
L63@P1: the pedestrian is composing the photograph (Levin et al., in press, Experiment 2).
L64@P1: Blindness to such real-world changes occurs even when observers know they are in
L65@P1: an experiment, provided that they do not know that a change is about to happen
L66@P1: (Levin et al., in press, Experiment 2). In all of these experiments change blindness
L67@P1: was defined as the failure to spontaneously report any aspect of the change when
L68@P1: asked open-ended questions. For example, after viewing a video of a change, participants were asked to describe everything that they had seen. For the real-world
L69@P1: changes, they were asked whether they noticed anything unusual and/or whether they
L70@P1: had noticed anything change.
L71@P1: Change blindness also occurs under laboratory conditions when participants are
L72@P1: actively looking for changes. For example, observers often miss changes to photographs provided that the change is made during a saccade (e.g., Grimes, 1996; Henderson & Hollingworth, 1999; McConkie & Currie, 1996), a flashed blank screen
L73@P1: (e.g., Pashler, 1988; Phillips, 1974; Rensink, O’Regan, & Clark, 1997; Simons,
L74@P1: 1996), a blink (O’Regan, Deubel, Clark, & Rensink, 2000), or some other visual
L75@P1: disruption (e.g., O’Regan, Rensink, & Clark, 1999; Rensink, O’Regan, & Clark,
L76@P1: 2000). When the original and changed version alternate repeatedly, separated by a
L77@P1: blank screen, observers often require many cycles of the original and changed image
L78@P1: to find changes (Rensink et al., 1997). The typical participant experience in both the
L79@P1: laboratory and real world experiments is consistent—they do not notice the changes.
L80@P1: However, intentional, laboratory change detection tasks and incidental, real-world
L81@P1-2: tasks might well reflect the operation of distinct encoding mechanisms (Simons &80 SIMONS ET AL.
L82@P2: Mitroff, 2001). In intentional tasks, observers actively try to detect changes. Consequently, they likely encode and retain as much information from each glance of a
L83@P2: scene as possible. In contrast, participants in incidental tasks are unaware of an impending change, so they are not actively searching for a change. Intentional tasks
L84@P2: measure how well observers can detect changes when they try to, whereas incidental
L85@P2: tasks might better reflect the amount of information retained and compared spontaneously under more natural conditions. We will return to this distinction in the general
L86@P2: discussion.
L87@P2: Given the variety of tasks that induce change blindness and the pervasiveness of
L88@P2: the phenomenon, both in the laboratory and in real-world situations, many researchers
L89@P2: have been tempted to conclude that change blindness reflects a failure to represent
L90@P2: the details of scenes (see Simons, 2000b, for discussion). We fail to detect changes
L91@P2: when they occur during a visual disruption, and that failure seems to reflect the visual
L92@P2: system’s assumption that the world is unchanging. A natural inference from this
L93@P2: assumption is that our experience of a stable and detailed visual world does not derive
L94@P2: from a detailed internal model of the world. Properties of objects generally do not
L95@P2: change instantaneously during disruptions (i.e., a conversation partner is unlikely to
L96@P2: be replaced by another person). Consequently, our visual system might simply assume that the world is stable without wasting effort representing much of the detail
L97@P2: of the world. Essentially, we rely on the world as an ‘‘external memory’’ (O’Regan,
L98@P2: 1992; see also Gibson, 1986/1979; Rensink, 2000a; Stroud, 1955), checking the details whenever we need them, and assuming that nothing changes without a signal.
L99@P2: Such a model might well explain our experience of a stable world in the face of
L100@P2: change blindness. Furthermore, the principles of minimal representation are consistent with a larger body of evidence from the study of visual integration across eye
L101@P2: movements (e.g., Irwin, 1991). However, the conclusion that we lack any representation of the world does not follow logically from a finding of change blindness (Simons, 2000b). Change blindness could occur even if observers formed a complete,
L102@P2: detailed, and precise representation of the original scene. For example, observers
L103@P2: could form representations of each glance at a scene but simply not compare those
L104@P2: representations from one instant to the next. Consequently, change blindness could
L105@P2: result from the failure to compare representations as well as from a failure to retain
L106@P2: a representation. Similarly, change blindness could occur if observers formed an accurate representation of the first view of a scene but never updated that representation,
L107@P2: essentially relying on their first impression. Furthermore, even if observers did not
L108@P2: form a representation that was accessible to verbal report, they might still form a
L109@P2: detailed and precise implicit representation of the scene that could not support conscious change detection (e.g., see discussion in Fernandez-Duque & Thornton, 2000).
L110@P2: Change blindness is entirely consistent with the existence of representations of the
L111@P2: initial and changed views.
L112@P2: Despite all of these alternatives, the most frequently proposed mechanism for
L113@P2: change blindness is that the second version of a scene simply masks or overwrites
L114@P2: the original version (Enns & Di Lollo, 2000; Rensink et al., 1997). Change blindness
L115@P2: occurs because any representation of the first display that could subserve change
L116@P2-3: detection is eliminated or disrupted by the appearance of the second display (or byCHANGE BLINDNESS 81
L117@P3: the visual disruption). This view is akin to the idea that change blindness results from
L118@P3: a failure to represent the pre-change scene. The overwriting account provides an
L119@P3: intuitive and plausible explanation for change blindness induced by flashing a blank
L120@P3: screen or by repeatedly cycling the original and changed image (the ‘‘flicker task’’).
L121@P3: In these tasks, observers intentionally search for changes, but the visual disruption
L122@P3: apparently prevents them from detecting the change. Phenomenally, the blank screen
L123@P3: seems to eliminate any persisting representation of the scene.
L124@P3: The overwriting account also seems to explain performance in some real-world
L125@P3: incidental tasks (Levin et al., in press). For example, in one study, pedestrians encountered an unexpected person change while providing directions, and after the interaction they performed a recognition memory task: they viewed 4 photographs, one of
L126@P3: which was of the pre-change assistant, and were asked to select the person they had
L127@P3: seen. Observers who noticed the change were able to select the pre-change assistant
L128@P3: better than would be expected by chance (M 5 63%). However, observers who
L129@P3: missed the change were substantially worse than those who detected the change (M 5
L130@P3: 26%), and not significantly better than expected by chance. A second experiment
L131@P3: confirmed that pedestrians who noticed the change were better able to recognize the
L132@P3: changed people and that pedestrians who missed the change were no better than
L133@P3: would be expected by chance. This difference in recognition performance suggests
L134@P3: that pedestrians who noticed the change had a better representation of the changing
L135@P3: feature(s) than did those who missed the change. However, even chance performance
L136@P3: on a recognition lineup task does not require the absence of a representation. Observers who failed to detect the change could have represented many details from the
L137@P3: first scene; a photographic lineup does not test all possible representations, and it
L138@P3: might not accurately reflect the amount of preserved information. Furthermore, given
L139@P3: that the pedestrians did not know they were in an experiment when the change occurred, they might have represented far less than they optimally could have represented.
L140@P3: In fact, another recent series of studies suggests that observers do retain some
L141@P3: details even when they fail to detect changes (Angelone, Levin, & Simons, 2001).
L142@P3: In these studies, observers viewed one of several videos of a person asking for directions. During a camera cut to a different angle, either the actor unexpectedly was
L143@P3: replaced by a different person or the properties of objects carried by the actor were
L144@P3: changed. After viewing the video, observers reported whether or not they had noticed
L145@P3: any changes (in response to a series of questions). They then viewed a photograph
L146@P3: of the post-change stimulus and tried to pick the pre-change stimulus from an array
L147@P3: of four photographs. Across experiments, between 45 and 95% of participants failed
L148@P3: to notice the change. Despite this large variability in the rate of noticing the change,
L149@P3: lineup recognition performance was relatively constant across experiments. Furthermore, in most conditions, recognition accuracy was comparable for those participants
L150@P3: who did and did not notice the change—both groups recognized the pre-change stimulus more frequently than would be expected by chance (between 40 and 60% of
L151@P3: the time, depending on the experiment). This finding suggests that even observers
L152@P3-4: who missed the change often did represent sufficient detail from the pre-change stimulus to be able to select it from an array of similar distractors. Had observers com-82 SIMONS ET AL.
L153@P4: pared this existing representation to the post-change scene, they could have inferred
L154@P4: the presence of a change.2 Thus, change blindness might have resulted from a failure
L155@P4: to compare existing representations. Note, however, that observers also could have
L156@P4: failed to represent the second actor. If so, then they would fail to detect the change
L157@P4: because they would have no features of the second actor to compare to the representation of the first actor (Simons, 2000b).
L158@P4: The goal of the experiments reported here is to explore whether change blindness
L159@P4: for a real-world, unexpected change can occur when observers have successfully
L160@P4: represented some of the changed details from the pre-change scene. That is, we sought
L161@P4: to explore whether change blindness can result from the failure to compare existing
L162@P4: representations (see Angelone et al., 2001). Instead of changing the identity of the
L163@P4: experimenter as the subjects were providing directions, in these studies we changed
L164@P4: a single object that the experimenter was holding. Following the interaction, we asked
L165@P4: a series of increasingly specific questions about the change, first giving the opportunity for a spontaneous report of the change (as in prior studies), and then providing
L166@P4: more detailed cues to see if the pedestrian would ‘‘discover’’ that they did have a
L167@P4: memory for the changed object.3 If change blindness results from complete overwriting of the first scene by the changed scene, then observers should be unable to retrieve
L168@P4: any details specific to the pre-change scene. In contrast, if change blindness occurs
L169@P4: without complete overwriting of the pre-change scene, then observers might well be
L170@P4: able to recall the properties of a changed object when prompted with a useful retrieval
L171@P4: cue, even if they did not spontaneously notice the difference.
L172@P4: Note, however, that observers might be able to recall details from the pre-change
L173@P4: scene even if overwriting does help to account for change blindness. For example,
L174@P4: the representation needed for change perception might be overwritten, leaving only
L175@P4: more abstract or verbal representations. If so, observers might then be able to report
L176@P4: the features of an object even if overwriting eliminated the representation necessary
L177@P4: for change perception. On the other hand, change detection via inference should still
L178@P4: be possible if observers can recall some details from the pre-change object. By arguing that preserved representations imply a comparison failure, we acknowledge
L179@P4: that change perception might differ from change inference and that overwriting might
L180@P4: better explain the elimination of change detection via perception. However, evidence

L147: 
L148: What is a leap second?
L149: 
L150: A leap second is a second added to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) in order to keep it synchronized with astronomical time. UTC is an atomic time scale, based on the performance of atomic clocks that are more stable than the Earth's rotational rate. Astronomical time (UT1), or mean solar time, is based on the rotation of Earth, which is irregular.
L151: There are two main reasons that cause leap seconds to occur. The first is that the duration of the atomic second was measured and defined by comparing cesium clocks to the Ephemeris Time (ET) scale, an obsolete time scale that defined the second as a fraction of the tropical year. The duration of the ephemeris second was slightly shorter than the mean solar second and this characteristic was passed along to the atomic second.
L152: If the atomic second had been defined with respect to the mean solar second, it is likely that leap seconds would have been required much less frequently. The second reason for leap seconds is that the speed of the Earth's rotation is not constant. It sometimes speeds up, and sometimes slows down, but when averaged over long intervals the trend indicates that it is gradually slowing.
L153: This gradual decrease in the rotational rate is causing the duration of the mean solar second to gradually increase with respect to the atomic second.
L154: For information about past leap seconds and the measured differences between UTC and UT1, please see the cite119†NIST Time Scale Data Archive .
L155: 
L156: How often do we have leap seconds?
L157: Leap seconds are added in order to keep the difference between UTC and astronomical time (UT1) to less than 0.9 seconds. The International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service (IERS), measures Earth's rotation and publishes the difference between UT1 and UTC. Usually leap seconds are added when UTC is ahead of UT1 by 0.4 seconds or more.
L158: At the time the corrections started in 1972, a necessary correction of ten seconds was made to UTC, and there have been leap seconds about every year and a half (on average). The current difference between UTC and UT1 is shown in our cite115†leap second archive web page .
L159: When do leap seconds occur?
L160: 
L161: Leap seconds have always occurred at the end of December or the end of June, on the last second of the UTC day. The designation of the sequence of seconds is:
L162: 
L163: 23h 59m 59s
L164: 23h 59m 60s
L165: 00h 00m 00s (the beginning of the following date)
L166: 
L167: So far, there have only been positive leap seconds. However, there is a provision for negative leap seconds if it becomes necessary due to changes in Earth's rotation. The designation of the sequence to remove a second would be:
L168: 23h 59m 57s
L169: 23h 59m 58s
L170: 00h 00m 00s (the beginning of the following date)
L171: 
L172: Are there benefits and/or detriments to adding leap seconds?
L173: By keeping Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) within one second of astronomical time, scientists and astronomers observing celestial bodies can use UTC for most purposes. If there were no longer a correction to UTC for leap seconds, then adjustments would have to be made to time stamps and legacy equipment and software which synchronize to UTC for astronomical observations.
L174: However, adding a second to UTC can create problems for some systems, including data logging applications, telecommunication systems and time distribution services. Special attention must be given to these systems each time there is a leap second.
L175: What is the future of leap seconds?
L176: Some proposals have been made to implement larger corrections like leap hours, which would occur much less often than leap seconds. Also, it has been suggested to stop corrections to UTC and publish the growing difference between UTC and UT1. The relatively small community that needs UT1 could then use the published values as a correction.
L177: Discussions of the future of leap seconds are ongoing at meetings of the Radiocommunication Sector of the cite120†International Telecommunication Union (ITU-R)†www.itu.int .
L178: How is a leap second related to a leap year?
L179: Leap seconds and leap years are both implemented to keep our time in accordance with the position of Earth. However, leap seconds are added when needed, based on measurements, and leap years are regularly occurring events based on set rules. During leap years, an extra day is added as February 29th to keep the calendar synchronized with the precession of the Earth around the Sun. Leap years are necessary because the actual length of the year is 365.2422 days and not 365.
L180: The extra day is added every four years to compensate for most of the partial day. However, this is a slight over-compensation, so some century years are not leap years. Only every fourth century year (those equally divisible by 400) is a leap year. For instance, 2000 was a leap year, but 1900, 1800 and 1700 were not.
